# Exact posterior correction and the heavy-fiber obstruction

This continues `candidate 41893e0c805c3bf4`. It keeps the ORIGINAL measure and derives the strongest correction obtainable from a cap's single posterior probability and the finite base likelihood ratios. Archive search found fractional-knapsack arguments for other allocation problems, but no saved posterior correction of this form. No general original-depth transfer is claimed.

## 1. Sharp scalar change of measure

Let pi_z>0 be the original base probabilities and p_z>0 the posterior probabilities. Both measures have the SAME uniform conditional law on each actual fiber. Write lambda_z=p_z/pi_z. For any measurable event H, including every closed ambient halfspace, its fiber capture fractions g_z lie in [0,1], and

    mu_original(H)=sum pi_z g_z,
    mu_posterior(H)=sum p_z g_z.

For 0<=q<=1 define

    B_(p,pi)(q)=min {sum pi_z g_z:
                     0<=g_z<=1, sum p_z g_z>=q}.        (1)

Then for ALL halfspaces

    mu_original(H)>=B_(p,pi)(mu_posterior(H)).           (2)

The minimum is attained. Sort lambda in decreasing order, equivalently pi_z/p_z in increasing order. Put P_j=sum_(i<=j)p_i and Pi_j=sum_(i<=j)pi_i. If P_(j-1)<=q<=P_j, the exact answer is

    B(q)=Pi_(j-1)+(pi_j/p_j)(q-P_(j-1)).                (3)

It is continuous, increasing and convex. Ties have the same slope and do not affect the answer. The exchange proof is elementary: moving posterior mass from a larger pi/p coefficient to an unfilled smaller coefficient cannot raise the cost. One obtains (3) after filling the cheaper fibers and at most one fractional fiber.

An exact dual form, useful without sorting, is

    B(q)=max_(eta>=0) [eta q-sum_z(eta p_z-pi_z)_+].    (4)

Indeed every feasible g has cost at least the displayed expression, since eta p_z g_z-pi_z g_z<=(eta p_z-pi_z)_+. Taking eta=pi_j/p_j at the fractional threshold in (3) gives equality. Endpoint cases q=0,1 follow directly. Similarly the sharp upper event envelope is 1-B(1-q).

Formula (1) is sharp among ALL measurable events: uniform positive-volume fibers are nonatomic, so the minimizing fractions can be realized by measurable subsets in each fiber. It is therefore the strongest scalar implication that forgets the joint geometry of the capture vector g. It need not be attained by an ambient halfspace in a particular fixed family. Actual halfspace sharpness is verified below where used.

For a fixed actual posterior delta-center Y, monotonicity in q gives the deterministic original certificate

    D_original(Y)>=B_(p,pi)(delta).                     (5)

This improves the crude delta/max lambda bound and has no probabilistic or optional-stopping premise.

## 2. Optimally corrected heavy-fiber localization cannot improve the original heavy-fiber bound

Let gamma be the ordinary fiber centroid guarantee (in this application gamma=Gamma_d). At a posterior-heaviest base i, p_i=p_max, its ordinary centroid is a posterior gamma p_max-center. But the feasible vector g_i=gamma and g_z=0 for z!=i shows

    B_(p,pi)(gamma p_max)<=gamma pi_i<=gamma pi_max.     (6)

This holds for EVERY positive posterior p, not merely Gaussian ones. At the original posterior p=pi the likelihood ratios are all one, B(q)=q, and the bound gamma pi_max is attained. Since the Gaussian parameter family includes a=0,t=0,

    sup_(Gaussian a,t>=0) B_(p(a,t),pi)(gamma p_max(a,t))
       =gamma pi_max.                                  (7)

Thus posterior heavy-fiber payment, followed by the sharp scalar change-of-measure correction, has exactly the same optimized strength as the ORIGINAL heavy-fiber certificate. It cannot close the original no-heavy regime.

The previously proved finite-time parity concentration implies only a lower bound on p_max. Its centroid certificate is bounded by gamma p_max pointwise, so applying (1) to that weaker certificate cannot evade (7). This is an exact limitation of this specified scalar localization scheme, not a prohibition on other localization invariants.

For a uniform prior on N bases, the identity is especially simple:

    B_(p,pi)(gamma p_max)=gamma/N                       (8)

for every p and 0<=gamma<=1, because gamma p_max lies in the first likelihood segment and its slope is 1/(N p_max).

## 3. Exact three-interval posterior and actual source selection

Use the actual family P={-1,0,1}, K_z=[-1,1], pi_z=1/3. By continuous reflection and exhaustive slope minimization, its global posterior depth is

    D_*(p)=max{p_-/2,p_+/2,p_0/2+min(p_-,p_+)}.         (9)

The maximum in EACH fiber is uniquely at its interval center. For the middle fiber, a sufficiently steep tilt can include the lighter endpoint fully and the heavier endpoint not at all, while choosing either continuous orientation. At a mark y this bounds depth above by

    p_0(1-|y|)/2+min(p_-,p_+),

strictly less than its center value for y!=0. This also supplies a direct uniqueness proof beyond reflection/quasiconcavity. Endpoint uniqueness follows by isolation of its own shorter half interval.

For Gaussian parameters put

    b=exp(-t/2) in (0,1],     r=exp(|a|)>=1.

After reflecting the base if necessary, the posterior is proportional to

    (b/r,1,b r).                                        (10)

The middle center is the unique posterior winner when

    b r < 1+2b/r,                                     (11)

and the positive endpoint center is the unique winner for the reverse strict inequality. At equality both centers maximize. Their ORIGINAL depths are respectively 1/2 and 1/6. Thus the actual original loss relative to the original optimal depth is exactly zero or 1/3 in the two strict regimes; it is not inferred from (1).

In terms of the likelihood oscillation R=max lambda/min lambda, an endpoint winner requires b r>1, so R=r^2. Condition (11) fails only if b(r^2-2)>r. Since b<=1, this requires r>2 and therefore R>4. Conversely, for EVERY R>4 choose r=sqrt R and b strictly between r/(r^2-2) and 1. This is a positive-time Gaussian tilt with a strict endpoint winner and original depth 1/6. At R=4 a tie occurs at b=1,r=2, but at strictly positive time no bad endpoint tie occurs with R<=4.

The same R can also have zero original loss: choose a=0 and b=1/R; then the unique winner is the middle center. Thus for R>4 the oscillation alone permits both original depths. For R<4 every posterior winner in this Gaussian family is the middle center. This is a sharp worst-selector threshold for this actual family, with the stated tie convention; it is not a universal likelihood-ratio theorem.

## 4. When the strongest scalar correction succeeds in the interval family

The OC target here is Gamma_1/k=1/4. Because the original prior is uniform, the first segment of B ends at original cost 1/3. Therefore

    B(D_*(p))>=1/4  iff  D_*(p)>=(3/4)p_max.            (12)

An endpoint-winning branch has D_*=p_max/2 and never passes (12). In the middle branch, substitution of (10) gives the exact criterion

    2+4b/r >= 3 max{1,b r}.                            (13)

Equivalently,

    b>=1/4,
    1<=r<=min{4b, [1+sqrt(1+12b^2)]/(3b)}.             (14)

These conditions already force the middle to win, so no extra branch assumption is needed. They give a nontrivial successful region of positive Gaussian times, but only when the ACTUAL global posterior depth (9), substantially stronger than heavy-fiber payment, is retained.

Examples:

* b=1/2,r=2 gives p=(1,4,4)/9, D_*=1/3 and B(D_*)=1/4 exactly.
* b=1/2,r=8 gives p=(1,16,64)/81, unique winner (1,0), D_*=32/81 and B(D_*)=1/6. The isolating halfspace on that endpoint realizes equality in (2), so this loss is sharp for actual halfspaces.
* Along a=0, the middle is always the unique winner and has ACTUAL original depth 1/2. Nevertheless, for b<=1/2 the scalar certificate is only B(1/2)=(1+2b)/6. It falls below 1/4 once b<1/4 and tends to 1/6. This gap comes from forgetting which three capture fractions can be produced by one halfspace through the middle mark.

Optimizing the exact posterior-depth certificate over a,t can therefore meet the target in this example; it reaches the original value 1/2 at the unaltered measure. This is not a new proof principle, since supplying exact posterior depth at a=0 supplies the original problem itself. In contrast, using only the posterior heavy/parity guarantee gives exactly 1/6 for EVERY tilt by (8), and optimization cannot reach 1/4.

## 5. Sharp cube times simplex calibration

Take P={0,1}^n, N=2^n, and every fiber equal to one d-simplex T. All prior masses equal 1/N and k=N. Every base is an exposed vertex. For any positive posterior p, a finite integer tilt isolates a fiber while retaining any specified continuous cut in it. Conversely its own mass is always captured at least to its ordinary depth. Therefore the maximum posterior mixed depth is EXACTLY

    D_*(p)=Gamma_d p_max,                              (15)

attained at a centroid of a posterior-heaviest simplex. The ordinary simplex centroid maximizes its depth at Gamma_d. Its original mixed depth is Gamma_d/N. Formula (8) gives

    B(D_*(p))=Gamma_d/N=Gamma_d/2^n                     (16)

for EVERY Gaussian tilt. A canonical centroid cap in a heaviest fiber, isolated by a base tilt, realizes equality in this change-of-measure bound. Thus the correction retains the sharp example exactly.

On binary bases |z|^2=sum z_i, so a Gaussian tilt is simply a product Bernoulli tilt with parameter vector a-(t/2)1. The time parameter creates no additional interaction. The success of (16) comes from N=k and the actual exposed-fiber geometry, while the three-interval obstruction has N>k and requires information shared across fibers.

## 6. Exact scope of the obstruction

The corrected posterior heavy-fiber certificate has optimized value Gamma_d pi_max, with no loss in this statement. Hence terminal closest-point parity, finite-time parity concentration, and the strongest likelihood-only event correction do not by themselves improve the original heavy-fiber bound. The actual interval example shows both failure and success of stronger correction depending on whether one retains the full posterior cap geometry.

There is also a general exact identity explaining the danger of optimizing with UNKNOWN exact posterior depths. Since a posterior deepest mark has original depth at least B(D_*(p)), while a=0,t=0 gives p=pi and B(q)=q,

    sup_(Gaussian a,t>=0) B_(p(a,t),pi)(D_*(p(a,t)))
       =D_*(pi).                                       (17)

The upper bound uses actual posterior centers and (5); the lower bound uses the unaltered measure. If one writes suprema rather than attained depths, the same proof follows by approximation and continuity of B. The analogous identity holds with one fixed mark Y throughout. Thus (17) is an exact re-expression of the original depth problem, not an independently computable certificate. The useful question is whether a new, weaker but accessible posterior estimate survives the correction; the heavy/parity estimate specifically does not improve its old original counterpart by (7).

A remaining localization route would need information beyond a posterior lower depth number and base likelihood ratios: for example, joint feasible cap profiles at one actual source. Such information is not supplied by the finite Gaussian identities. Nothing here asserts a global failure of every possible localization method or an OC counterexample.
